talks.title: #RomHack2021 - Luke Hinds - sigstore, software signing for the masses!
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #RomHack2021 - Luke Hinds - sigstore, software signing for the masses!.
talks.summary:
Speaker Background and Motivation

Luke Hinds of Red Hat's Office of the CTO describes sigstore as a lockdown-era project addressing secure software supply chains. His team works on supply-chain security and he volunteers on the Kubernetes security response team.

Supply Chain Anatomy

A typical chain runs from developer commits through human review, CI build systems, security scanners, and artifact publication to downstream consumers—including critical sectors like health, banking, and infrastructure. Sonatype reported a 650% increase in supply-chain attacks, mostly targeting open source.

Common Attack Patterns

Hinds explains rollback and replay attacks where proxies serve outdated vulnerable package versions, and key-compromise attacks exploiting trust-on-first-use models that make undetected key theft difficult. He also covers the SolarWinds incident, where a backdoored signed DLL was accepted because its signing certificate was compromised.

Sigstore Direction

The talk positions sigstore as the response to these signing and trust failures, though the available transcript ends before detailed technical coverage of the project.

talks.title: #RomHack2021 - Dirk-jan Mollema - Breaking Azure AD joined endpoints in zero-trust environments
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #RomHack2021 - Dirk-jan Mollema - Breaking Azure AD joined endpoints in zero-trust environments.
talks.summary:
Azure AD and Zero Trust Basics

Dirk-jan Mollema clarifies the talk targets Entra ID cloud identity, not on-prem Active Directory. Zero trust combines user and device identity signals for access decisions.

Device Join Models

Azure AD Join, registered BYOD containers, and hybrid joined devices each create device objects manageable via Intune or on-prem GPOs, with different trust boundaries.

Join Flow Internals

Device registration posts CSR, transport keys, and loosely validated metadata to Microsoft's enterprise registration service, returning a tenant-signed device certificate and local admin group changes.

Attacker Opportunities

Mollema previews abusing primary refresh tokens, unofficial device registration, and Intune-admin MFA bypass techniques against joined endpoints in zero-trust architectures.

talks.title: #RomHack2021 - Folini - Proteggere l'accesso al voto online con l'OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #RomHack2021 - Folini - Proteggere l'accesso al voto online con l'OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set.
talks.summary:
Speaker

Christian Folini, 15-year ModSecurity production veteran and OWASP CRS co-lead, presents a defensive blue-team case for protecting high-assurance systems—notably Swiss internet voting—with ModSecurity plus the Core Rule Set.

WAF reality

Commercial WAF markets exploded after PCI DSS mandated presence (not effective configuration); Folini compares WAFs to seat belts—baseline protection buying time, not a silver bullet replacing secure code and patching.

Stack

ModSecurity is an Apache/nginx module applying byte-level inspection and regex rules; CRS is the dominant open ruleset, reused by many commercial products, blocking roughly 80%+ of Burp-driven exploits in benchmark tests while skilled attackers may still persist.

Voting use case

For online voting's high-security needs, CRS on ModSecurity is positioned as the practical open-source path versus expensive commercial offerings that often wrap the same engine without added value.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Christian Folini, co-lead of the OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set (CRS) project, delivers a presentation at RomHack 2021 on utilizing Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) to secure internet voting infrastructure in Switzerland. Folini outlines the practical defensive philosophy of WAFs, illustrating how open-source rule engines provide robust defense-in-depth against web application attacks. He examines the unique political, accessibility, and cryptographic considerations surrounding Swiss direct democracy and details how CRS is deployed at high paranoia levels to protect online voting portals against exploitation and service disruption.

Key Topics:
- Web Application Firewall defensive philosophy and the OWASP Core Rule Set
- Automated attack mitigation metrics and CRS paranoia levels (PL 1–4)
- Societal and cryptographic trade-offs of Swiss internet voting
- Hardening e-voting access points with strict anomaly scoring

Technical Details:
Folini introduces the defensive role of WAFs, comparing them to automobile seatbelts: while they cannot eliminate underlying coding flaws, they mitigate impact, buy operational response time, and deter opportunistic adversaries. The OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set (CRS) operates as a standardized, open-source rule engine running on ModSecurity (or modern lean proxies like Nginx and Envoy). Folini notes that while commercial WAFs are costly and frequently market proprietary machine learning capabilities, approximately two-thirds of commercial offerings rely on CRS under the hood. To demonstrate empirical effectiveness, Folini shares benchmark data running Burp Suite with advanced plugins against a vulnerable application; over 4.5 million automated scan requests generated over 1,000 vulnerability alerts across 40+ bug classes. Installing a default CRS deployment blocked more than 80% of exploit attempts out of the box, completely neutralizing automated SQL injection, Local File Inclusion (LFI), and Remote Code Execution (RCE) vectors.

To achieve protection suitable for critical infrastructure, CRS implements four paranoia levels (PL 1 through PL 4). While PL 1 provides baseline protection with virtually zero false positives, higher paranoia levels introduce increasingly rigorous regular expressions, strict character whitelisting, and lower anomaly score thresholds. In high-security environments, deploying CRS at PL 3 or PL 4 requires fine-tuning rules to the application's expected HTTP parameter formats, thereby preventing advanced evasion techniques such as HTTP parameter pollution, chunked transfer encoding anomalies, and complex cross-site scripting (XSS) payloads.

Folini contextualizes this technical hardening within Switzerland’s 20-year history of internet voting pilots. He addresses classical cryptographic objections formalized by Bruce Schneier—namely, the tension between maintaining secret ballots through encryption and ensuring election transparency and recountability without encryption. However, Folini details four compelling Swiss requirements driving e-voting adoption: enfranchising the 10% of Swiss citizens living abroad who face unreliable postal services; providing private, unassisted voting for visually impaired and quadriplegic citizens guaranteed under the constitution; eliminating the 0.5% to 10% rate of formally invalid hand-marked paper ballots; and preventing physical ballot box tampering (referencing a recent fraud case where an election official replaced 200 paper ballots). To safeguard these high-stakes e-voting portals, administrators deploy ModSecurity CRS configured with strict paranoia levels, isolating authentication workflows and protecting backend election servers from web exploits and automated denial-of-service barrages.

Key Takeaways:
Organizations operating high-value public web services must implement defense-in-depth using well-maintained, open-source WAF rule sets like OWASP CRS rather than relying on unverified proprietary commercial claims. Deploying CRS at elevated paranoia levels (PL 3 and PL 4) coupled with application-specific tuning provides aggressive filtering against automated scanners and sophisticated injection attacks. Securing digital democracy requires balancing end-to-end cryptographic verifiability with hardened web access layers that ensure both system availability and ballot confidentiality.

talks.title: #RomHack2021 - Antonio Morales - Fuzzing Apache HTTP Server for fun (and CVEs)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for #RomHack2021 - Antonio Morales - Fuzzing Apache HTTP Server for fun (and CVEs).
talks.summary:
## Fuzzing Apache httpd at Scale

GitHub Security Lab researcher Antonio Morales details fuzzing the Apache HTTP Server at RomHack, aiming to improve open-source security through automated testing. His work targets C/C++ codebases using AFL++ and custom tooling, with Apache httpd as a flagship case study yielding multiple CVEs.

## Architecture and Attack Surface

Apache's lifecycle spans startup (config parsing, library loading), operation (privilege drop from root via setuid, request processing), and cleanup. The Apache Portable Runtime provides cross-platform memory pools, I/O, threading, and shared memory—each module representing fuzzing entry points.

## Incremental Module Coverage

Morales describes enabling modules progressively in httpd.conf, stabilizing fuzzing harnesses before expanding scope until all modules run reliably. This incremental approach prevents crashes from misconfiguration from masking deeper bugs in rarely loaded extensions.

## Custom HTTP Mutators

Default AFL bit-flip mutators poorly suit structured HTTP traffic. Morales built protocol-aware custom mutators generating valid request grammars, dramatically improving crash discovery rates. Code is published on GitHub for researchers extending coverage to other network-facing parsers.
